heuristics.rule: When negotiating salary as an H-1B candidate, identify the exact dollar threshold between your current wage level and the next one, then anchor your salary request to that threshold
heuristics.condition: When you are an H-1B candidate and your current offer sits at Wage Level II or III...
heuristics.action: ...research the DOL prevailing wage thresholds for your specific SOC code and geographic area, then frame your salary request as 'To qualify for Wage Level III/IV, my salary needs to be at least X for this occupation in this location'
heuristics.because: This argument is structurally independent of market data and ties the salary request to a concrete immigration benefit — moving from 2 to 3 lottery entries is a 50% increase in selection probability, which is quantifiable value the employer can understand

heuristics.rule: Use lottery-risk avoidance as a retention argument once you are already on an approved H-1B at Level III or IV
heuristics.condition: When negotiating a raise or retention package as an existing H-1B employee at Wage Level III or IV...
heuristics.action: ...frame the turnover cost argument explicitly: replacing you means re-entering the weighted lottery with no guaranteed selection, representing a 50%+ probability of failing to hire the replacement at all
heuristics.because: Under the wage-weighted system, the employer has already cleared lottery selection risk — replacing an existing H-1B holder means absorbing that risk again, which is a quantifiable and asymmetric cost to the employer

heuristics.rule: Treat each salary dollar as worth more than face value if it pushes you across a wage level threshold
heuristics.condition: When an H-1B candidate is close to a wage level boundary (e.g., $15,000–$30,000 away from Level III)...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize closing that gap over negotiating equivalent amounts elsewhere in the comp package (e.g., signing bonus), because the marginal immigration value of crossing the threshold exceeds the dollar value alone
heuristics.because: A wage level increase buys both purchasing power and a structurally higher lottery selection probability — a dual return that US citizen candidates do not receive from the same salary increase

decision_factors.factor: Current wage level classification (I–IV) of the offer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines the number of lottery entries (1–4) and directly sets selection probability; the difference between Level II and III is a 50% increase in odds
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the employer's immigration attorney which wage level the LCA will be filed at, or independently look up the DOL OEWS prevailing wage tables for the specific SOC code and metro area

decision_factors.factor: Proximity of offered salary to the next wage level threshold
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If you are $10,000–$30,000 away from the next wage level, the immigration value of that increment is disproportionately high relative to its dollar value
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Cross-reference the offered salary against DOL prevailing wage data for the role's SOC code and location to calculate the exact gap to the next threshold

decision_factors.factor: SOC code and job duties classification
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Wage level is tied to duties and SOC code, not salary alone — a higher salary without matching duties does not automatically move you to a higher wage level
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review the job description against DOL wage level definitions; confirm with the employer's immigration counsel what SOC code and level the LCA will use

decision_factors.factor: Whether the candidate is already on an approved H-1B vs. entering the lottery
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The weighted lottery rule only affects new lottery selection; existing approved H-1B holders are not retroactively affected, which changes the negotiation dynamic entirely
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine current visa status: is this a first-time H-1B filing, a transfer, or a renewal? Only new cap-subject filings face the weighted lottery

decision_factors.factor: Legal challenge risk to the final rule
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Court injunctions could delay or block implementation before the FY2027 lottery, making wage-level-based negotiation arguments premature or moot
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Monitor immigration law news sources for injunctions filed against the rule between publication (December 2025) and effective date (February 2026)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Employers who have already invested $3,000–$8,000 in fees and attorney costs for an existing H-1B employee face higher replacement costs under the new system, strengthening the candidate's retention leverage
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether you are an existing sponsored employee (high employer sunk cost + lottery risk) vs. a new hire candidate (lower sunk cost)

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer at Wage Level I or II without negotiating up to the next threshold
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Under the new system, a Level I candidate has approximately half the lottery odds of a Level IV candidate — accepting a lower wage level is not just a compensation concession, it is a probabilistic concession on immigration outcome
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Entry-level H-1B candidates who are unaware of the wage-weighted system and negotiate only on compensation grounds without considering lottery probability

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Framing a salary negotiation purely around market data rather than wage level thresholds
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may successfully negotiate a $5,000–$10,000 increase that stays within the same wage level, gaining purchasing power but zero improvement in lottery selection probability
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B candidates who do not research DOL prevailing wage thresholds before negotiating and therefore leave the most asymmetric value on the table

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating a higher salary without confirming the job duties will support the higher wage level classification
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The employer's attorney may file the LCA at a lower wage level regardless of salary, meaning the candidate receives more pay but no additional lottery entries — and may face LCA compliance issues
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who assume salary and wage level are directly correlated and do not verify the duties-based classification with immigration counsel

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on the wage-weighted lottery rule as settled law for long-term career planning
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The rule faces potential legal challenges that could result in injunctions before the FY2027 lottery, leaving candidates who negotiated specifically around wage levels without the expected immigration benefit
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have structured their entire compensation negotiation strategy around the wage-level lottery differential before the rule survives legal challenge

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating salary as if you are a US citizen — optimizing only for total comp without accounting for wage level thresholds
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most salary negotiation advice is written for US citizens or permanent residents; H-1B candidates apply the same frameworks without adjusting for the asymmetric value of crossing a wage level boundary
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate may secure a modest raise but remain at Wage Level II, missing a 50% increase in lottery selection probability for the difference of $15,000–$30,000 in salary
warning_signs: Candidate references only market data (Levels, Glassdoor, competing offers) without mentioning DOL prevailing wage thresholds
Candidate negotiates for signing bonus or equity without first maximizing base salary to the next wage level threshold

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming a higher salary automatically means a higher wage level classification
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The link between salary and wage level seems intuitive but is legally incorrect — wage level is determined by job duties and SOC code, not pay rate alone
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate negotiates a higher salary expecting more lottery entries, but the LCA is filed at the same wage level because duties did not change, resulting in no improvement in selection odds
warning_signs: Candidate has not consulted or asked the employer's immigration attorney about the wage level of the LCA
Candidate conflates 'I earn more than prevailing wage' with 'I am at a higher wage level'

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to use the retention/lottery-risk argument when already on an approved H-1B
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on their own risk (fear of rocking the boat, visa dependency) rather than recognizing the employer's now-quantifiable cost of replacing them under the weighted lottery
failure_patterns.consequence: Existing H-1B holders leave significant leverage unused in salary reviews, accepting below-market compensation when they have asymmetric retention power
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I can't negotiate aggressively because I depend on my employer for my visa'
Candidate does not frame the cost of their replacement in terms of lottery re-entry risk when asking for a raise

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the wage-weighted lottery as a done deal without monitoring for legal challenges
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Final rules feel permanent once published; candidates and employers may not track litigation that could result in injunctions before the effective date
failure_patterns.consequence: Career and salary decisions made around the wage-level system may be premature if the rule is enjoined before FY2027 registration
warning_signs: No mention of monitoring immigration litigation news between December 2025 and February 2026
Employer or candidate is making long-term hiring decisions based solely on the rule without a contingency plan

diagnostic_questions.question: What wage level (I, II, III, or IV) will the employer file the LCA at for this role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the candidate's baseline lottery entry count and whether there is an actionable path to negotiate up to a higher level
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If Level III or IV: how close is the offered salary to the Level IV threshold? Is there room to negotiate further?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Level I or II: what is the exact salary threshold to reach Level III for this SOC code and location, and is the gap closeable through negotiation?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is this a new cap-subject H-1B filing, a transfer, or a renewal of an existing approved H-1B?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the weighted lottery rule applies at all — existing approved H-1B holders are not subject to re-selection and have different negotiation leverage
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If new cap-subject filing: wage level is critical for lottery odds — prioritize wage level threshold analysis
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If existing approved H-1B: the retention/lottery-risk-avoidance argument is the primary lever — focus on replacement cost framing

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate know the DOL prevailing wage for their specific SOC code and metro area, and the salary breakpoints between wage levels?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the candidate can make a structurally grounded wage-level argument, or is relying only on market comp data which is insufficient for H-1B negotiation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: verify that the duties of the role actually support the higher wage level classification, not just the salary
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: candidate needs to research DOL OEWS data or consult with an immigration attorney before entering salary negotiation

diagnostic_questions.question: How much has the employer already invested in this candidate's immigration process (fees, attorney time, prior filings)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Quantifies the employer's sunk cost and the incremental risk they face from turnover under the new lottery system, which calibrates how strong the retention argument is
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If significant investment: the retention premium argument is strong — frame replacement cost explicitly including lottery re-entry risk
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If early stage with no prior investment: retention argument is weaker; focus on wage level threshold and market comp arguments instead

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the candidate aware that wage level is determined by job duties (SOC code) rather than salary alone?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the candidate risks negotiating a salary increase that looks like a wage level upgrade but isn't, due to misunderstanding how the DOL classification works
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: confirm they have verified with immigration counsel that the duties support the higher level classification before using it as a negotiation anchor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: candidate must understand this before negotiating — a higher salary without matching duties classification yields no additional lottery entries

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B candidates are in a weak negotiating position because they depend on employer sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: Under the wage-weighted lottery, employers who have already sponsored an H-1B at Level III or IV face a quantifiable and asymmetric cost to replacing that employee — they must re-enter a lottery where there is a 50%+ chance of not getting selected at all
industry_realities.implication: Existing H-1B holders at Level III/IV have stronger retention leverage than most realize and should frame salary negotiations around the employer's lottery re-entry risk, not their own visa dependency

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary negotiation for H-1B candidates is the same as for US citizens — maximize total comp using market data
industry_realities.actual_reality: Each salary dollar has asymmetric value for H-1B candidates if it crosses a wage level threshold, because it simultaneously increases purchasing power and lottery selection probability — a dual return unavailable to US citizens
industry_realities.implication: H-1B candidates should prioritize closing the gap to the next wage level threshold above other comp components (signing bonus, equity) when near a boundary, and should always negotiate with DOL prevailing wage data in hand

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher salary means you will be classified at a higher wage level for H-1B purposes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Wage level is determined by the DOL's assessment of job duties against the SOC code definition — salary alone does not determine wage level. An employer can pay above prevailing wage while still filing at Level I if the duties match Level I
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must confirm both the salary and the duties-based wage level classification with immigration counsel; negotiating salary without confirming the LCA wage level may produce no improvement in lottery odds

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery is random and salary is irrelevant to selection odds
industry_realities.actual_reality: As of the FY2027 lottery (registration March 2026), the system is wage-weighted: Level IV applicants have 4 entries vs. Level I's 1 entry, more than doubling selection probability at the high end and halving it at the low end
industry_realities.implication: Any career or salary advice for H-1B candidates that does not account for the wage-weighted lottery is materially incomplete as of early 2026; wage level optimization is now a core component of H-1B career strategy

industry_realities.common_belief: The wage-weighted lottery rule is a proposed regulation that may or may not pass
industry_realities.actual_reality: The rule was finalized on December 23, 2025 (Federal Register document 2025-23853) and takes effect February 27, 2026 — it is settled law as of early 2026, not a proposal
industry_realities.implication: Advisors, career coaches, and candidates referencing this as 'proposed' or 'pending' are operating on outdated information; decisions should be made as if the rule is in effect unless a court injunction is issued

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses only market data (competing offers, Levels.fyi, Glassdoor) to justify a salary request, treating the negotiation identically to how a US citizen would approach it
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Layers the DOL wage level threshold argument on top of market data — anchors the salary request to the specific dollar amount needed to cross into the next wage level for the exact SOC code and location
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The wage level threshold argument is structurally independent of market data and ties the salary request to a concrete, quantifiable immigration benefit the employer can verify — it is a stronger and less contestable anchor

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of what determines wage level
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes wage level automatically increases with salary — believes negotiating a $20,000 raise will move them from Level II to Level III
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows wage level is tied to job duties and SOC code classification, not salary alone — verifies with immigration counsel that the duties support the higher level before using it as a negotiation argument
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Negotiating a salary increase that stays at the same wage level produces zero improvement in lottery odds; the senior approach closes the loop between salary, duties, and LCA classification

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Perception of visa dependency in negotiations
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats visa dependency as pure weakness — avoids aggressive negotiation because 'I can't afford to lose sponsorship'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Recognizes that visa dependency is bidirectional — the employer who has already sponsored an H-1B at Level III/IV also depends on avoiding lottery re-entry risk, creating a retention premium the candidate can explicitly price
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The junior framing leaves significant leverage unused; the senior framing converts a perceived weakness into a quantifiable retention argument that is grounded in the employer's actual replacement cost

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Relies on secondhand career advice that may reference the wage-weighted lottery as 'proposed' or 'under consideration,' without verifying current legal status
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Verifies the rule's status directly against primary sources (Federal Register, USCIS) before making decisions — knows it was finalized December 23, 2025 with an effective date of February 27, 2026
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Acting on outdated regulatory information leads to miscalibrated negotiation strategy; the senior approach ensures decisions are grounded in the actual legal landscape, not stale secondhand summaries
